headline: Race Sees First Bonito, Black Point Sea Bass Won't Quit
subhead: Bluefish keep the rods bent while the stripers wait on bait to bunch up ahead of Sunday's full moon.
body_markdown:
Ran into one of the Niantic drift boat mates at the tackle counter Tuesday and the first thing out of his mouth wasn't fluke or bass — it was bonito. Said a couple of the smaller center consoles working out toward the Race picked up their first false albacore-looking fish of the season skipping bait on the surface, and by his description they were bonito, not albies, pushing in off that Block Island wave everybody's been talking about all August. That's early for this stretch of water but it tracks — the whole Eastern Sound has been running warm, New London reading 69.4 on the surface, and that's plenty of water for bonito to keep working west along the reefs toward Fishers Island and into the mouth of our zone. Worth having a small metal or an epoxy jig rigged on light tackle if you're running out that way, because that push doesn't usually stick around long once it shows.

The bigger story for the weekend, though, is the moon. We flagged this last week — said the building moon toward full would tighten up feeding activity and strengthen the tide over the next 72 hours, and the fleet is starting to see it. Current's noticeably harder on both the flood and the ebb through Twotree Island Channel and around Hole-in-the-Wall, and that's pushing bait tighter against structure instead of letting it spread out over the flats. Full moon lands Sunday/Monday, and if the pattern holds like it usually does this time of year, the next few days should sharpen up the bite on everything holding near rock — sea bass, porgies, and the blackfish that are starting to show up on the drift boat bycatch.

Sea bass are the one thing nobody's complaining about right now. Black Point and the rock piles off McCook Point are holding fish in that 30- to 45-foot range, and the party boats working Hole-in-the-Wall have been putting together solid mixed bags — sea bass to 4 pounds mixed with keeper porgies on the same drift. Squid strips and clam belly on a high-low rig is still the standard, but a few mates are running Gulp Peanut Butter and jelly swimming mullets on light jig heads when the current's ripping and bites get finicky. Best window has been the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide, when the current slows enough that a bait or jig actually sits still on bottom instead of getting swept sideways off the structure.

Fluke are doing exactly what they're supposed to do the first week of September — thinning out. Niantic Bay and the inside grounds near the river mouth gave up decent numbers all summer, but those doormat-class fish are sliding out toward the deeper structure around Twotree Channel and the edges off Hole-in-the-Wall ahead of the fall push offshore. Anyone still chasing them should be working 25 to 35 feet of water on the outgoing tide, dragging white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails slow along the bottom. The numbers are there if you find the right piece of structure, but it's not the wide-open June bite anymore — call it a grind-it-out fishery now, not a limit-out fishery.

Bluefish have been the most dependable thing going and that's held true right through the week. Peanut bunker and small bunker schools are still stacked up in Niantic Bay and along the edge off McCook Point, and the blues have been chopping through them most mornings and again toward dusk. Diamond jigs with a tube teaser, or bigger poppers thrown at working birds, have been getting bit consistently. This activity should hold strong right through Labor Day week — warm water's kept these fish aggressive and spread out all along the Sound, and nothing in the forecast suggests that changes soon.

Striped bass are the one piece still lagging behind where the calendar says they should be. Reports out of Black Point and the river mouth have fish around — guys marking bunker schools on the meter and picking off a few bass working the edges — but nobody's calling it a blitz yet. Water's still sitting in that high-60s range, warm enough to keep the bigger schools loose and non-committal instead of balled up and vulnerable. The building moon and the stronger current that comes with it should start squeezing those bunker schools tighter over the next several days, and once that happens the bass usually follow. If you want a shot at one now, live bunker on a fish-finder rig fished tight to the bait schools at first light, or a bucktail worked slow along the current seam off Black Point on the last of the ebb, are the better bets.

Looking at the next few days: expect the sea bass and porgy bite to stay the most consistent thing in the zone, especially on that top-of-tide window at Hole-in-the-Wall and Black Point. Keep an eye on the bluefish schools tracking the bunker — that bite isn't going anywhere through the holiday. And if the moon does what it usually does, the stripers could start tightening up into something more aggressive by the weekend. Worth having a rod rigged for bunker just in case that switch flips.
